interest: Shows Japan's strict control over foreign access to military-industrial sites like Sumitomo's cable works, amid July 1937's Sino-Japanese war outbreak.
keywords: Sumitomo Electric Wire and Cable Works
overview: This file, classified under U.S. State Department decimal file 894.22711 (relating to the admission of foreigners to military institutions, workshops, and services in Japan), contains correspondence from 1930 and July 1937. The earliest record (January 1930) is a letter from Assistant Secretary of State Francis White informing the Secretary of War that the Japanese Government consented to a three-month observation visit by Major William B. Duty of the Philippine Scouts (Air Corps) to the Japanese Army Air Service. The remainder of the file, dated July 1937, centers on John K. Roosevelt, Vice President of All America Cables, Inc., who sought State Department and consular intervention in Osaka to secure official Japanese permits to inspect the manufacture of submarine cable at the Sumitomo Electric Wire and Cable Works. The State Department telegraphed the Tokyo Embassy to instruct the Osaka Consulate to provide the necessary certification for Japanese authorities, which Roosevelt subsequently acknowledged with thanks.
